lessons.title: Comparer deux lieux
lessons.objective: Comparez deux lieux d’étude avec plus, moins et aussi ; employez meilleur et mieux dans le bon contexte.
lessons.foundationTie: Reuses Core 18 places, Core 20 classroom context and Core 21 descriptions; adds comparative choices.
lessons.focus: plus/moins + adjectif + que; aussi + adjectif + que; meilleur pour + nom

grammar.explanation: Place plus or moins before an adjective, then que before the second thing: la bibliothèque est plus calme que le café. For equality, use aussi + adjective + que: cette table est aussi grande que celle-là. Meilleur is the adjective for a better book or place; mieux is an adverb for doing something better. The adjective agrees with its noun: confortable stays the same in the feminine.

model.more: La bibliothèque est plus calme que le café.
model.less: Le café est moins loin que l’école.
model.equal: Cette table est aussi grande que celle-là.
model.better: Mon livre est meilleur pour les débutants.

grammar.caution: The pinned English phrase “less far away” is retained as moins loin, although le café est plus proche is often more natural in conversation. The source objective is truncated (“Use más .”); the full French comparison sequence is inferred from the pinned examples and must be independently reviewed.

lessons.scene: Deux amis choisissent entre la bibliothèque et le café pour étudier.
dialogue: La bibliothèque est plus calme que le café.|The library is quieter than the café.
Le café est moins loin que l’école.|The café is less far away than the school.
Cette table est aussi grande que celle-là.|This table is as big as that one.
Mon livre est meilleur pour les débutants.|My book is better for beginners.
La chaise rouge est plus confortable.|The red chair is more comfortable.
Quel endroit est meilleur pour étudier ?|Which place is better for studying?
lessons.speaking: Compare the library and café with a classmate. Say which is quieter, which is less far from school, and which table is as big as another. Recommend a beginner’s book, then ask which place is better for studying and confirm your partner’s choice.

words.note: French est covers identity, condition and location; there is no ser/estar distinction.
Est can describe condition or location; se trouve highlights location.
La can be an article or an object pronoun, depending on syntax.
Pour + noun or infinitive is common; afin de + infinitive is more formal.

lessons.title: Remplacer ce qu’on cherche
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Direct object pronouns: Lo, la, los and las replace a direct object and agree with it: el libro → lo; las llaves → las.
lessons.objective: Remplacez un objet déjà nommé par le, la, l’ ou les et placez ce pronom avant le verbe conjugué.
lessons.foundationTie: Builds on Core 14 articles and Core 22 school objects; distinguishes an article from a direct-object pronoun.
lessons.focus: le, la, l’, les before a conjugated verb; object gender and number

grammar.explanation: French direct-object pronouns replace a person or thing receiving the action: le livre → je le trouve; le sac à dos → je l’ouvre; les cahiers → je les range. Put the pronoun before the conjugated verb. Le and la become l’ before a vowel or mute h: je l’ouvre, elle l’utilise. Les works for plural objects of any gender. The article follows a noun; the object pronoun replaces it.

model.book: Je cherche le livre et je le trouve.
model.backpack: J’ai le sac à dos et je l’ouvre.
model.notebooks: J’achète les cahiers et je les range.
model.keys: J’ai besoin des clés, mais je ne les vois pas.

grammar.caution: French les is plural for both masculine and feminine; it does not preserve the Spanish los/las contrast. In “J’ai besoin des clés,” des is required after de; les later replaces clés. The final question uses l’ for an unspecified singular item; the English source does not identify its gender.

lessons.scene: Deux camarades rangent leurs affaires avant de partir en cours.
dialogue: Je cherche le livre et je le trouve.|I look for the book and find it.
J’ai le sac à dos et je l’ouvre.|I have the backpack and open it.
J’achète les cahiers et je les range.|I buy the notebooks and put them away.
J’ai besoin des clés, mais je ne les vois pas.|I need the keys, but I do not see them.
Ana a le crayon et elle l’utilise.|Ana has the pencil and uses it.
Tu l’as, toi ?|Do you have it?
lessons.speaking: Pack a school bag with a classmate. Ask about the book, backpack, notebooks, keys and pencil. Name each object once, then replace it with le, la, l’ or les. Confirm whether your partner has the missing item.

words.note: La can be a feminine article, a feminine direct-object pronoun, or “her” as an object; identify its role from context.
J’ai besoin de means “I need”; the French construction includes de.
Les is a plural article or direct-object pronoun for any gender; it can mean “them” in this lesson.

lessons.title: Dire à qui l’on donne
lessons.sourceObjectiveEnglish: Indirect objects: to whom?: Me, te, le, nos and les can identify the recipient: le doy el libro a Ana.
lessons.objective: Dites à qui s’adresse une action avec me, te, lui, nous ou leur devant le verbe.
lessons.foundationTie: Extends Core 23 object-pronoun placement to recipients, contrasting “what?” with “to whom?”.
lessons.focus: me, te, lui, nous, leur as indirect-object pronouns; à + recipient

grammar.explanation: An indirect-object pronoun can mark the recipient: je donne un livre à Ana → je lui donne un livre; Luis me prête un crayon; la professeure nous explique la question. Place the pronoun before the conjugated verb. Lui is singular for either a man or a woman, and leur is plural for any gender. In French, “je lui donne un livre à Ana” can occur in colloquial dislocation, but beginners should use either “je donne un livre à Ana” or “je lui donne un livre” to avoid a redundant recipient.

model.Ana: Je donne un livre à Ana. Je lui donne un livre.
model.students: Nous donnons les cahiers aux élèves. Nous leur donnons les cahiers.

grammar.caution: The English source glosses “me / myself” and “you / yourself” are broad. Reflexive meaning belongs to separate uses; here me and te refer to recipients. Lui/leur differ from Spanish le/les; do not add the named recipient after the pronoun in formal beginner models.

lessons.scene: Des élèves partagent livres et cahiers avant un cours et vérifient qui reçoit quoi.
dialogue: Je donne un livre à Ana.|I give Ana a book.
Luis me prête un crayon.|Luis lends me a pencil.
Je t’écris un message.|I write you a message.
La professeure nous explique la question.|The teacher explains the question to us.
Nous donnons les cahiers aux élèves.|We give the notebooks to the students.
Tu peux me prêter ton livre ?|Can you lend me your book?
lessons.speaking: Share class materials. Tell a classmate that you give Ana a book, ask to borrow a pencil, write a message, explain who receives the notebooks, and request the classmate’s book. Repeat two exchanges with lui or leur replacing the named recipient and confirm who receives each item.

words.note: Me marks a recipient here; myself is a different reflexive use.
Te marks a recipient here; yourself is a different reflexive use. It elides to t’ before a vowel.
La can be an article or a direct-object pronoun depending on syntax; this lesson focuses on recipients.
Les is a plural article or direct-object pronoun; the indirect plural recipient pronoun is leur.
Élèves means pupils; étudiants is typical for university students.
